utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, both witnesses from Bosnia are here but literally only just. Therefore, I'm not going to name either of them, because there's always the possibility that there will be an application by one or other for protective measures. The witness producing the tape I've spoken to very briefly, and he's expressed some concerns about being rushed into the process of being a witness without a little more discussion. He's speaking to Mr. Lopez-Terres, I hope, at the moment, but before any time comes for him to give evidence, I'd ask for a short adjournment to check that he's content with what he's doing and also to check on his position so far as protective measures is concerned. The other witness is also being spoken to and I hope will be ready this morning, being seen and should be ready this morning. In those circumstances, I suggested to Mr. Stein that it might be convenient for him to address his argument in relation to admissibility of the tape, obviously without reference to the name, and to see how far we can progress without the need to call a witness becoming a live issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the witness whose statement we have been handed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- with -- just literally a witness statement, not a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. In this case, the statement itself is prepared effectively in the form of a summary. It's a very recent statement, and it's very succinct. It also contains, on the third sheet, an index of calls to be found on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be simplest for you, briefly, to introduce what the evidence is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will then read the statements, and we'll hear the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you got the other shorter statement, but that can be made available to you, and it may be that Mr. Stein will be happy to proceed on the basis of that being an accurate account of the history of matters, at least for the purposes of his argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with that, the shorter statement we don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I thought you had been supplied. It was our intent to read it out. It's six paragraphs. It suffices, for my purpose. We can put it on the ELMO. I just don't have extra copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Copies will be obtained. I can, with the usher's assistance, lay the body of the document on the ELMO and read from it for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Stein, we'll hear the Prosecutor open the case, as it were, and then we'll hear your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I shan't name this witness just in case he comes to give evidence and does seek protective measures. So we won't let his signature be shown. But he said this in his statement, that he -- "I am a telecommunications engineer by profession. On the 1st January, 1993, I was appointed head of the High Frequency Equipment at the PTT in Zenica. Part of my duties included liaison with the 3rd Corps in Zenica. "In the beginning of 1993, I was informed by members of my staff that there was something unusual on the "official line" of the PTT which ran between Vitez and Busovaca. The official line was an internal line normally used by PTT staff in emergency situations to deal with technical problems within the network. However, it appeared that the line was being used by people in Busovaca for military matters. "I informed Edin Husic at the 3rd Corps headquarters in Zenica. Edin asked for the line to be diverted to the office of the 3rd Corps. I returned to my office and instructed my staff to divert the line. The line was disconnected from the inductor switchboard in the Zenica office to the Technoprojekt building, the headquarters of the 3rd Corps. "The PTT did not supply any equipment or technical assistance to the 3rd Corps in relation to this matter. "At this time, the telephone lines going to and from Busovaca had been cut and this official cable which ran via the PTT in Zenica was the only possible line to use. "I do not know how long this line was diverted to the 3rd Corps in Zenica. I do not know when it became undiverted." The other witness is able to produce the tape. The Court has his statement. In summary, he sets out how the diverted phone call line was monitored; how small cassette tapes were made of certain conversations; how those recordings were transferred to a standard sized tape, reviewed by him, the witness; how he, the witness, took another copy of that tape; how the original copy of the tape, which no doubt should have gone to archives, became mislaid; and how it was discovered very recently that his retained tape might be of value, and thus it was produced. The tape itself, of which the Court has transcripts, is plainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we don't. We haven't had the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If you don't have transcripts, they'll be coming your way. I'll just check it before they do come. Yes, the transcripts are coming your way, and originals -- not the originals, the B/C/S versions as well. Thank you. The tape has been transcribed and translated by the official department here. There is, I think, one potential for confusion arising on the first page of the English translation of the transcription, where it says, "Side B." If the Court goes to the third page of the witness statement, the Court will see that the listing begins on side A and runs down to side B, and it may be, if and when we listen to the tape, that it simply should read, on the first page of the transcript, "Side A" and not "Side B" at all, because the recorded conversations starting on the first sheet of the transcription do appear to match the index provided by the witness. The witness is able to identify voices, and they were recorded on the cover of the cassette at the time. They may all be of considerable interest, but the one that is of starkest and most obvious value is the first one on the tape. And again since argument on admissibility is being raised, it may be better, as we're in open session, to deal with things in this way: to invite the Court to turn to the second page of the transcript as an example of the significance of the tape and to note that Voice 6 is Kordic, Voice 7 is Blaskic, and simply to read the first seven lines of that tape for a piece of material of the very greatest possible significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Excuse me. That, it seems to me, would be putting the cart before the horse. We're challenging the admissibility both as to legal matters, search and seizure, as well as to what we would call chain of custody, or reliability, or providence, as in other jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not challenging it on the grounds of eavesdropping or something of that sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are. Very well. You don't want us to read the tape; is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's the short of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean normally we need to know what the evidence is about before we can rule on it. We're not a jury.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it may be that there would be no objection to the proposition that, if admissible or if not inadmissible, the Defence accept entirely that this is a document -- this is an exhibit of great potential relevance and materiality, and if they do, then I needn't introduce the matter further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It may be the fairest way to deal with it. We'll assume that it's material and important. If there are to be these challenges, let's make sure I have, speaking for myself, that I have the background. This was a line owned by the Zenica PTT which was diverted to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. At the time, it was the only remaining effective telephone line between Busovaca and Kiseljak. It was, I think, a line for use by PTT staff rather than a domestic line. It was obviously thus a line that was being used for their purposes by, for example, Blaskic and Kordic, in the absence of other communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have that. It was diverted to the office of the 3rd Corps. The line was then monitored and tapes made of significant conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In this case, so that we have the picture precisely, I haven't had time to read the evidence in detail, but it seems that the monitor handed the witness a tape, of which he made a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then made a further copy for another gentleman whose name appears in paragraph 9. I don't know whether he's protected or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, of course, the gentleman in paragraph 9 is the person whom we referred to yesterday and who is one of the sources of intelligence that such a tape existed, which led to the search for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how does the tape come here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Physically, it was produced last year to an investigator and lawyer from this team and brought by them, I think, to this building and then processed in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who produced it to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness himself. If one turns to paragraph 14 and 15, the tape is dealt with as to its labelling production and onward production to us. But in any event, the witness is here, able to identify the tape, both as to the physical tape itself and as to the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll hear the objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, may I be clear. I'm talking, as I stand, relative to the legality only as opposed to the providence or the reliability, although some of the remarks may be overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful if you deal with both.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. First, it's clear from the statement read into the record that the individual was working as a liaison with the 3rd Corps in Zenica, and that's at paragraph 1 of his statement. As part of that liaison capacity, he suggested to the witness who is ready to testify that this tape might be -- these conversations might be of interest. And indeed having listened, this particular officer, with the TO, decided to accept the invitation. He was then working for the 3rd Corps as head of the Intelligence Unit. His duties included Electronic Warfare Unit, including obtaining and analysing information on the enemy, who at the time were the HVO, and the Republika Srpska, the JNA, and the HV. That's set out at paragraph 4 of his statement. Some but not all of the conversations listened into after the transmission was diverted were recorded; some but not all. The decision was based, apparently, on the monitors who were listening to the conversation and instructions given to them by their officers. Apparently, again according to paragraph 7, and it's unexplained why, the original recording was done on micro-cassettes, the minis, as we call them -- they're the small ones -- then collected and transferred to regular cassettes for reasons unstated, except, apparently according to paragraph 7, the paucity of available of mini cassettes. The time of the calls was not reported, and the cassette was eventually handed to the witness who was in waiting. The details of each of the intercepts, the dates, were apparently put on a list on the outside of the body of the cassette, although we've not been provided with that list. In all, there were 13 conversations recorded between the period January 24, 1993 to February 25, 1993. Thirteen have been recorded for posterity, if you will, and that's as per paragraph 9 of the statement you have before you. Paragraph 12 is significant because in 1996, this witness received orders from Sarajevo relevant to all documents and anything else that may be useful for investigation of war crimes committed during the conflict, and as per paragraph 13, his -- and I may quote specifically: "My department was tasked to make a list of all items and information gathered. Included in this collection of information was a further copy made in 1996 of my tape that I compiled in 1993. In July 1996, I handed over all my archives to my successor Hasim Saric. I know nothing further about the copies of the tape." So Mr. Saric apparently had the tape, and at least according to this paragraph, no copy was kept by the witness, although later he is inconsistent on this point. In November of 1999, specifically November 19, in Vienna, during a chance encounter or discussion relevant to war crimes, he was having a conference with his Chief, Mr. Mustafa Music -- and this is paragraph 14, there are two paragraph 14s, this is the first paragraph 14 -- in which documents that apparently missing were discussed, and the witness volunteered that he had a copy of the tape at issue and the next day handed that tape to Mr. Music. So apparently these paragraphs are somewhat inconsistent. Either there was one copy delivered and he had none or he had a copy. He handed it to Music. Music held that tape until 3 December, 1999, when there was a meeting between the witness and Colonel Nermin Eminovic from the sector of security and intelligence, in which the tape was again shown to the witness and he recognised the tape as being the tape handed to Music on 20 November, 1999. On 4 December, 1999 in Zenica, the same tape was handed by someone to Sue Ellen Taylor and Mr. Lopez-Terres from the Prosecutor's Office, and this witness identified the tape as the same number he had handed over earlier. The tape contains 14 -- I may have said 13 earlier -- conversations intercepted between January and February, originally record on the micro-cassette and late re-recorded by this witness onto this tape. So consequently, it's clear from the evidence that either in 1996 when he handed the tape over to Mr. Saric it was out of his control or, alternatively, he kept a copy of a copy. And that's significant. He kept a copy of a copy in his possession until 1999, when it was given to Mr. Music, who in turn gave it to Mr. Nermin Eminovic, who in turn apparently gave it to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. So clearly it was out of this witness's custody and control either between July 1996 and November 20, 1999 or, alternatively, between November 20, 1999 and December 3, 1999. Whatever the situation, it is clearly a copy of a copy. The original also being on cassettes. So this is the third generation of the tape, the original being the mini cassettes, the first copy being made and turned over pursuant to instructions in 1993, this witness apparently had kept a copy at one point, and this is either the third or fourth generation of the tape. So those are some of the issues relative to providence. When we hear from the witness, of course we can resolve others. I will say, parenthetically, save for the first tape, save the one that the Prosecutor says is most important, the tapes are filled, and the transcript so indicates, with the words "inaudible." There are huge gaps in the tape that you simply can't hear. We find that fascinating. It's fascinating that the words of Mr. Kordic that the Prosecutor finds significant, no one seems to have any problem hearing, they're perfectly audible, but other times they're not so audible. So the quality of the tape and the manner of its recordation and why some words are heard and not, and why the tape went on and off, of course, is an issue. But I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's an issue which we're going to have to decide on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But that's your first objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. More significantly, however, and I did do a skeleton argument about this, and I'll hand it up now, this is clearly in violation of the law as it existed in the former Yugoslavia. Under the law as it existed in the former Yugoslavia, and I would certainly defer to my three colleagues, all of whom were Judges under the Yugoslavian legal system, Article 83(3) of the Yugoslav Criminal Code, which is cited at paragraph 4 of my skeleton argument, allowed only the Police to collect wire transmissions, and even then it was for limited purposes. These transmissions needed to be collected with a Court Order. There is clearly no court order in this case, and clearly the Police did not involve themselves in this particular situation. I note that the record doesn't adequately reflect the citation. The citation is Article 83(3) of the Yugoslav Criminal Law. On April 11, 1992 the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted legislation incorporating, by reference, all of the laws of the former Yugoslavia. The citation for that, unfortunately, is found at paragraph 4 of my pleading. It's inappropriate to be there. It should be under paragraph 5, but the citation of authority is Article 60 of the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, found at the Sluzbeni List, RBIH, number 2, page 299, April 11. Clearly, therefore, what appears before the Court is something obtained without court approval, in violation of the laws of the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as of 1993. Putting aside the issues of quality and the circumstances, the fortuity of the tape arising, which require evidence, this is evidence that the Prosecution clearly should not be allowed to use under Rule 95. If Your Honours agree with me that these tapes have been seized illegally, the question becomes whether admitting them in this proceeding would run afoul of our rule that says: "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast doubt on its" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just pause here and consider the situation as it was on the ground. Suppose, for the sake of the argument, that the conversation was about shelling Zenica. And it doesn't matter which side, for the sake of the argument. One side has information that the other side is about to shell or indeed conduct any operations, and they know that such information -- there may be conversations which they can tape. Are you saying that they should have gone to a court and -- or spoken to the Police and gone to The Court before they taped the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski has much to say as an expert on this area, and if Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would like, Mr. Stein, you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm going to. Believe me. He's very anxious to add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My short answer to your question, Judge, is I'm not so naive as to believe that during a war there are all kinds of interceptions by satellite, by other means, et cetera. That's part of war. On the other hand, the issue becomes having seized all these things through -- because of war, are they admissible here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But your first argument is that this was illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's right. What the army did illegally, if you will, in the throes of a civil war, theoretically should have an exception because of a war, as I understand Your Honour's question. That's the first thing that ran through my mind. However, it is the position of the Prosecution, and they have an expert who will give evidence shortly named Ribicic, that the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina were alive and well in 1992 and 1993. He's going to use that as a basis for his opinion relative to the legality of the HR H-B and other Croatian institutions. So at first blush I ask myself the same or similar question that Your Honour posed. Then I thought about the Prosecution's position on this subject and rethought our position, and that's why we're here today. I don't think for two seconds that both sides, three sides, five sides, the intelligence community and whoever else was interested wasn't conducting electronic warfare. Of course it was, but the question is whether we should accept it here. Again, I guess the answer is what is done in war is illegal by definition, if you will, on some level. I mean killing and spying and all the things that go with conflict in a civilised world doesn't exist, so you have to decide, "Do you have laws or don't you have laws," and the Prosecution contends, based on the contention we apply, that the laws of Bosnia did apply, that if they are going to tap phones, as they clearly did, they needed authorisation. But the second prong of the law is that even if it's illegally tapped, it's not admissible under Bosnian law in any proceeding unless the defendant agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, its inadmissibility under Bosnian law wouldn't necessarily make it inadmissible in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right, and that's why I cite, if Your Honour pleases, Rule 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 95. But even before you get to 95, the governing norm, as I understand it, is relevance, subject to prejudice. That, as I understand it, is the governing norm, and that is reflected in Rule 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the mere fact that it is inadmissible under domestic law doesn't make it inadmissible here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With respect, sir, the last words of 95 are "seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The proceedings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If Your Honour agrees, assume it's relevant, assume it's accurate, assume it's material, but assume it's illegally obtained. Then Your Honours would be giving improviture [phoen] tacit approval to illegal conduct by admitting it into evidence as something we do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not necessarily. It doesn't mean that you are approving the conduct. The only question you have to decide in a case of this sort is whether it's admissible in these proceedings. It's not the duty of this Tribunal to discipline armies or anything of that sort. Its duty is to determine whether the accused is guilty or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and as Your Honour articulates it, that's half, if you will, of the basis of the exclusionary rule, discipline and future conduct of those whose evidence is no longer allowed. That is not certainly something that I'm going to argue in this setting. However, the tacit approval, by allowing said evidence into this record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm not accepting that we are approving or disapproving the conduct. All we are deciding is whether this evidence is admissible under Rule 95. And the test is, as 95 sets out: "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability." That is the first part which you're going to argue when you've heard the evidence. "... or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." And it's the integrity of the proceedings, as I understand it, that you're saying would be damaged if we admitted this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By way of a homily example, if a confession, which we're all familiar with, was literally stomped out of an individual or prisoner, the confession is relevant, it's probative. It may not be reliable, but I dare say the Court would not admit it under the circumstances by which it was obtained. That's one example of illegality imposed on a court, and I would argue in that situation, as I do here, the Court ought not to take that evidence because of the manner in which it was collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the point, as to whether we should admit it or not, not whether we approve or disapprove the conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly, but the reason for taking it or not taking it is based on circumstances extraneous to the proceedings at some level but, on the other hand, important to the role of courts in society everywhere, which goes, I think, to Judge Robinson's issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to address a question to the Office of the Prosecutor, to Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice, there is the tape, the transcript of the tape. There is the testimony on the whole issue around the tape. The witness or some other person, could they tell you what was the use made or the information drawn outside the tape and the use made of that information, because if we limit ourselves to this particular case, we have had a lot of intelligence information and military information taken left and right which ended up in the milinfosums or in various intelligence reports, military reports, and in that case we didn't discuss the legality of the source, of the provenance, how they were obtained. We were satisfied by hearing the testimony of persons who produced that information. Is there any testimony on the information itself, on the contents, because for the moment we just have testimony on the actual procedure by means of which this tape was obtained, how it was recorded and re-recorded, and so on. Is there anything, any testimony, regarding the contents and what was done with the contents or, rather, the information contained on the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the moment, the statement isn't explicit on the topic, but it makes it clear, at paragraph 7, that the conversations being taped were for purposes of the Electronic Warfare Unit, and we can see from those selected that they all have the characteristic of being relevant to tactical or strategic matters in hand at the time. And although I haven't asked him specifically, I can be pretty confident that the witness would tell the Court that, of course, this was intelligence gathered for the purposes of conducting the war and that that was the way it was used, insofar as it was used at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the problem is to learn, and perhaps you could do that, whether that witness is ready to tell the Court, outside the recording itself, whether he could testify on the contents and what was done with that information -- the substance of the information, and what was done with that information. Could he do that, not limiting himself to the actual tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He certainly can do that, and to some degree he covers that. For example, Your Honour will have noted at paragraph 8, as His Honour Judge May also observed, that one particular conversation which has a particular obvious potential military significance was communicated forthwith to a named person, indeed a named person from whom we might otherwise have heard about the contents of the tape or might otherwise hear about the contents of the tape. And he sets out there the reason why he was communicating that particular conversation to the person named. There's no difficulty in my finding out. Indeed, if Mr. Scott is able to leave us briefly, if you would like us to deal with this swiftly, he can, I'm sure, find out, in general terms, further whether any of these particular tapes were communicated to individuals for particular purposes. But it's pretty obvious that it was all communicated, or insofar as it was communicated, it was as in paragraph 8, which was communicating to Military Commanders for their use. We can look at other conversations in detail to see the sort of topics that were being covered, which are exactly the sort of topics that we have covered with intelligence reports coming from other agencies, convoys, obstructions of convoys, matters of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, that is my question. Couldn't you cover this information through testimony rather than through the transcript of the tape itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that here Your Honour is missing something or I am. The fact that the contents of the tapes were communicated to other people and that other people would be able to say, "I was informed that this, that, or the other thing was likely to happen," is capable of being of value to you, but it's not the real value of this tape. This tape, and of course you're not being allowed to look at it at the moment, but this tape shows the sort of things that Kordic said, the sort of instructions he gave, the position he occupied, the authority he had, and it is therefore the best evidence of that. It's exactly the same as, if not rather better than, a person standing beside a defendant, coming to the Court and saying, "I heard the defendant," take a different example, "give an instruction to attack Sarajevo," something like that. This is the best conceivable evidence of that sort, and its value -- well, its value may be many and various, but its greatest value is in showing what Kordic said and, by so saying, did. And so it goes beyond, to this extent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I would like to defer to Mr. Naumovski for a moment, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Naumovski, we may be prepared to accept -- I don't know, perhaps the Prosecution can assist us if there is any argument about this -- that the law in Bosnia at the time was, as stated by Mr. Stein, following the Yugoslav law, and we may be able to accept, for the purposes of this argument, that this interception was illegal for those purposes. I don't know if that's accepted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think we'll be in a position to accept that. We've only had the skeleton very recently. The law is not that simple, and there may be derogation of rights in times of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But it's always possible to proceed on two alternative bases, because if there is no ground for objection even if it were illegal, then we needn't descend to the other detailed argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear Mr. Naumovski. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll be as brief as possible. This is what I wanted to say. I accept what my learned colleague Mr. Stein has just said, and what he said is correct. In the area of the former Yugoslavia, and that same law held true in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 because the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took it over as its own on the basis of a set provision, which my colleague quoted, it was only the Police, only the Civilian Police, the organs of internal affairs, as we like to call them, had the possibility of amassing intelligence from citizens, and as this was regulated by Article 151 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, the matter in hand, that is to say, the monitoring of other peoples' phone calls, was not regulated by that particular law but by a bylaw and its provisions which regulated the functioning of the Internal Affairs organs. According to those bylaws and provisions, the Police, in a legal way, were able to tape somebody's telephone calls only with Authorisation from the Internal Affairs Minister. And if I may respond to a question raised by you too, Mr. Stein, in relation to the assumed shelling, the only legal way in monitoring a telephone call of that nature, which could have an effect on proceedings, was exclusively by permission received from the Minister of Internal Affairs. And I don't want to tire you there, because there are certain details and finer details within that, but the essential thing is that the Civilian Police and the internal organs were the only people who could have undertaken such an action. No other body was permitted to do this, not only because it is a process which could not be applied in the criminal proceedings against an accused but because, and I feel that this is something that Your Honours should be aware of, as I say, but because primarily any unauthorised taping and taping and recording was a criminal act in itself. There was a sentence of imprisonment to be enforced if this were done by an official, and it was a term of imprisonment of up to three years. That is Article 60 of the Penal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which stipulates that. Similar provisions existed in all the other Republics of the former Yugoslavia. Therefore, we had two situations, in point of fact; first, the tape that was recorded, it is absolutely impermissible not only for the former Yugoslavia but throughout the world as well. All countries, as far as I know, and Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, for example, have taken over in substantial practice with what was prevalent in the world. And on the other hand, what was done represents a criminal act, in fact, because the recording was made, the tape was made by an unauthorised individual who abused his official capacities. Perhaps my translation of article -- of Rule 95 is not exactly in line with the English text, but as far as I'm able to understand Rule 95, it seems to be that it would be -- well, I don't know. Perhaps I'm going to use a strong word, but it would be immoral and it would do a great deal of harm to the proceedings in this case if we were to actually admit something which was the result of a criminal act for which a prison sentence can be enforced. So not only because it cannot be used in this particular proceeding but also because it is the product of a criminal act. That is how I understand the meaning of Rule 95 as expounded here. Of course, the question remains, the one that Mr. Stein touched upon, the authenticity and reliability of the tape, because it is a copy of a copy, if I have understood it correctly, it is not the original, which, once again, leads to other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to hear evidence about that. So we don't need to hear any argument about it at this stage. Now, we've heard Mr. Stein on Rule 95, and I thought, Mr. Naumovski, you were going to address us upon the Yugoslav law or the law of Bosnia, which you have done. Now, is there anything else you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are a whole series of finer points, Your Honour, with which I did not wish to tire you, but it all boils down to two basic principles, the ones that I have explained; that is to say, that on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, you could do recordings of this kind exclusively if you had permission to do so from the Minister of the Interior. Today, for example, as I have already said, the Prosecutor must ask permission from a court of law, and then it is the court that can permit conversations to be taped in a given case and proceedings against an individual. So even according to the provisions that hold true today, you cannot tape all phone calls, only the phone calls of individuals whom you suspect to have committed a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, because personally I must admit I'm ignorant regarding the legislation in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we know, in general terms, that this type of rule knows exceptions, specifically, as I think the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor reminded us a moment ago, at times of armed conflicts, wars, the ruptures of peace. Are there such exceptions envisaged to this rule? There is no need for us to hear argument about the rule itself, but are there exceptions when such recordings are permitted, when we know that a -- normally permission from a court of law is required. But we know there are exceptions. In the legislation that you are referring to, are there any exceptions envisaged for exceptional circumstances in specific cases? That is what is of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me answer in the only way open to me. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by a provision having the law of force, a decree with the law of force, took over the Law on Criminal Procedure, and that decree law was published in the Official Gazette of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 11th of April, 1992. In taking over this old Law on Criminal Procedure, one that was held true in Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina changed certain articles of that decree law; however, not the article which relates to the internal affairs organs and their conduct, Article 151, in fact, on the Law of Criminal Procedure. And quite honestly, to be quite frank, I haven't got the provisions in front of me and I don't know if anything was done in taking over the bylaws as well and the provision of those bylaws; that is to say, whether the competencies of the organs of the Ministry of Internal Affairs have perhaps been expanded in any direction. But I should like to repeat once again that this was possible only within the organs of the Interior. Nobody is outside the Internal Affairs organs; that is to say, the Civilian Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just wanted to make a brief comment on the significance of Rule 95, which represents a very important development in international humanitarian law. The presence of Rule 95 is entirely due to the developments that have taken place in human rights law since 1945. For example, you'd have no such provision in the regime that governed the Nuremberg trials. This is entirely due to the importance which contemporary international law attaches to human rights. But it has to be properly understood. The concept of serious damage to the integrity of the proceedings is one that connotes, in my view, shades of conduct, shades of illegality. It is not illegality which will seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. I, for one, would never sanction the admission of evidence which is derived from a confession that is procured by intimidation or by force. I would consider that that is conduct which would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings, but each case has to be judged on its own merits. True, there are some kinds of illegality which, within the contemplation of Rule 95, would call for its application, but it is not every illegality, not every act. Rule 95 challenges what, in Mr. Stein's jurisdiction is called the concept of the fruits of the poison tree, but there are really shades of conduct, and we have to examine each case on its own merits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I cannot deal comprehensively with the question of legality, having only just received the skeleton argument. It would be astonishing, however, if Commanders of the Electronic Warfare Unit, properly conducting the war that it was their duty to conduct in defence of the people they represented, were vulnerable both at the time and thereafter to criminal process for doing that which they did for strategic or tactical purposes. I note that this was not the tap of a private line, for what it's worth. Of course, if the issue of legality were ever to be taken to the limit, thought would have to be given to the fact that the line that was being used was probably itself being misused, for it was the PTT line, somehow taken over by Blaskic and Kordic and others using it for military purposes, not a private line. Mr. Guariglia, in anticipation of what might come today, helped me -- and I'm grateful to him -- by some citations from the code, the prevailing code, which, in any event, may provide exceptions to what is being argued should apply, and under 205, Article 205, where there is a requirement that telephone conversations can only be recorded pursuant to the orders of an investigative Judge, there may, I think, be exceptions where the circumstances are such as to involve disproportionate difficulties. It's worth noting that under Article 210, there's provision made for the seizure of material that would otherwise require a search warrant, again in particular circumstances. So if it's ever necessary to look at the matter in detail, it may well be (A) that this isn't a tap; (B) that the fact that the parties concerned were using somebody else's or misusing somebody else's line; and (C) provisions within the code itself would make this well outside any alleged illegality. On top of that I make two or three other points and that's all I think I need stay at this stage. What is involved here, of course, is not material procured by the Office of the Prosecutor or investigators or anything of that sort, to pick up his owner Judge Robinson's point about confessions. Indeed, at the time these conversations occurred, this Tribunal hadn't even been thought of. What is at stake here is the use by this Tribunal of material seized -- well, produced and then retained by others. And the Chamber will well know there are many jurisdictions where such material, whatever the circumstances, if it's original generation or seizure, will be admitted. Second point, also building on His Honour Judge Robinson's explanation of the origins of Rule 95 and the development of humanitarian law, the conventions upon which our present humanitarian law are built themselves contain provision for derogation in times of war, and they might have to be looked at again with some care if the overall question of this alleged illegality had to be considered. It's worth observing, although to some degree this stems from the reading of the transcripts themselves, it's worth observing that there is no question of privacy here, nor any expectation of privacy, and indeed the tape recordings make it clear when the parties started to be oblique in their references and cautious in their terminology, that they were expecting or countenancing the possibility of being overheard. It's also worth having in mind that we've already had evidence from an open-session witness, General Merdan. He spoke of overhearing a tape recording of a conversation, and at that stage, there was no challenge to his evidence on grounds of admissibility. In our respectful submission, there is simply nothing in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. There's nothing in the illegality point, and Rule 95 is not in any sense offended. On the contrary, this is evidence, as we know, because it's conceded, of relevance and value and should be before the Tribunal. And unless it's now desired to test admissibility on grounds of provenance, for which evidence is required, perhaps it would then be in a private or closed session. We would invite the Court to reject this argument on the basis that, at this stage, it's quite impossible to test fully whether any law was breached, and indeed Mr. Naumovski candidly acknowledges he doesn't have all the law at hand, but the Chamber could deal with it either on the basis of saying even if illegality were established, nevertheless, there is no breach of our Rules. Alternatively, it could say that in seeking to exclude, the Defence should be subject to the burden of proving illegality, and they haven't proved it. But by one means or another, we would invite you to say there is nothing in this point and move to the next stage of either the argument on admissibility or, alternatively, simply to take the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you want a short adjournment before calling the witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I've been told that he would seek protection in the form of pseudonym and face distortion. So I'll have to get details of that, in any event, to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're, in fact, nearing the time for an adjournment. We'll hear any reply, briefly, at this stage, and then we'll consider what to do next. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall be really brief. The Prosecution wishes to underline that the important thing is whether this was a private conversation or not and whether it was a private line or not and that everything should be reduced to legality. I think I was precise in my statement. I said that one point is the fact on the Law on Criminal Procedure that was in force in the territory of the former Yugoslavia would consider such a tape impermissible, unacceptable in court proceedings which, in my view, makes it illegal. But what is important is also that I underline that this tape was obtained by committing an act of crime. Let me refer to the first sentence from this article, which will show you that it doesn't matter which line is being tapped and whose conversation, and I quote: "Who uses special equipment to tap or record a conversation by using special means, conversation that is not addressed to him." I think it is convincing enough to confirm that this tape was obtained by a person committing a criminal act. That is why, I think, that the product of a criminal act cannot be used in this court or in any other court of law as evidence, nor can any judgement be based on it or rely on it. That is all I wanted to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, in the legislation that you are familiar with, there are surely situations specific to war. In times of war, certainly there is humanitarian law which is applied, and that's why we're here, but there are a certain number of exceptions to the regular legislation in force regarding behaviour. You know that. In all legislations there are exceptions for times of war, for emergencies, for times of conflicts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. As regards this situation you're referring to, Your Honour, by the Law on Criminal Procedure, it is prescribed through the competencies envisaged for the Internal Affairs bodies. In those exceptional situations, the bodies of Internal Affairs -- that is, the Police - for the needs of an investigation are authorised to collect information from all and sundry sources but, again, in a lawful manner. For instance, they could call citizens for interviews. They could record certain persons' telephone conversations with the permission of the Minister of the Interior. They could search apartments. They could identify people, ask for identity papers, and many other means were available to them. However, the information obtained by the Police, on the basis of an interview with a citizen, could not be used as evidence in proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, that is not the question. I was asking you about a situation when there is a break in authority. There are several authorities that were confronted amongst each other. The situation you're referring to means that there was one authority that was in jeopardy and takes exceptional measures. You're not going to say that the enemy is going to ask permission from the opponent's Minister of the Interior to record a telephone conversation in a situation of war. There is a break in authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour, but precisely because of that rupture, that break in authority -- just a moment, please -- the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, headed by President Alija Izetbegovic, bridged that gap by passing, adopting a decree with a law of force on the takeover of the Law on Criminal Procedure, and this decree regulates criminal procedure under exceptional circumstances; namely, as in all countries, in the Territory of the former Yugoslavia too, laws were passed by the Assembly, but this was a constitutional exception. In the case of a state of war, the Presidency is allowed to adopt decrees with the force of law. So bridging this gap, if I can call it that, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina took over this Law on Criminal Procedure, amended it to some extent, adjusting it to the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, but it did not amended those articles that I referred to, Articles 151, 83, 84, and so on -- 83, rather. Therefore, I consider this to be my answer to your question, Your Honour Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This application is in two parts under Rule 95, and I deal with that part which has been argued so far; namely, that the admission of this evidence would be antithetical to or would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. Our ruling on this part, of course, has no bearing at all as to our ruling on the second argument, which relates to the reliability of the evidence, again under Rule 95, and about which we will hear evidence and rule after the adjournment. But turning to the issue, as I have explained it, of the first part of the argument, I might say at the outset that the Chamber is disappointed that it has not been provided with full material as to the law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on this particular topic. Parts have been referred to but not the whole. Were this ruling to turn on that, we would have to adjourn it. We would invite counsel, in fact, instruct them, that in future if reference is to be made to these matters, it must be done fully and the matter must be fully ventilated before us. But we can rule on this basis, that even if the illegality was established, and we're not saying it has been because, as I say, we haven't heard full argument, but even if it was, we have to decide whether this is evidence obtained by methods which -- the admission of which would be antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. We have come to the conclusion that the evidence obtained, as put before us in this way, evidence obtained by eavesdropping on an enemy's telephone calls during the course of a war is certainly not within the conduct which is referred to in Rule 95. It's not antithetical to and certainly would not seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. In those circumstances, as far as this argument is concerned, we reject it. We will deal, after the adjournment, with the argument as to whether the way in which it was obtained casts substantial doubt on its reliability. You'll be ready, Mr. Nice, with your witness at half past 11.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. There is, as I indicated, an application for a measure of protection, so may we reconvene initially in closed session and I'll make the application as soon as you like, half past 11.00 or twenty-five past, whatever you'd prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will reconvene at half past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I discussed the issue of protection further with the witness. He is entirely content to give evidence with no protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give the Chamber, please, your full name?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: My name is Edin Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you presently a Colonel in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, having been most recently in Vienna, and currently waiting to take up a new post elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did your career start in 1986 at the military academy in Belgrade, becoming a lieutenant, working in Zagreb until 1991, when you deserted the JNA and went to Zenica, where, as a volunteer, you joined the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In December 1992, when the Territorial Defence ceased to exist and the 3rd Corps of the BiH came into existence under the command of Enver Hadzihasanovic, did you join that Corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I did, yes. I was seconded from the district Territorial Defence staff to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you work in the intelligence section, and did that section have the assistance of soldiers from the Electronic Warfare Unit, and did your duties include the obtaining and analysing of information on the enemy?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time, did the enemy count the HVO, the Army of the Republika Srpska, the JNA and the Army of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we perceived them as such, that is, all those who were a threat to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've set out in your statement the area of your interest generally, but for these purposes, is it the case that your area of interest included Busovaca, Kiseljak and other places in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In January 1993, did you receive information from a man who we need not name but who worked in the Zenica post office?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a result of what he told you, were arrangements made for a telephone line to be diverted from the Zenica post office to your intelligence unit, and did you thereafter monitor that line?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The line was diverted to the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know the number of the line or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think that particular line had any number of its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you believe the line to be?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that man told us it was a line which covered conversations between military persons, that is, that it was a military line, as they called it. And we then agreed to survey it, but we had no advance knowledge as to what we might hear, what might happen, or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who monitored the calls as they came through to your department? Don't give the names, but give the description of the people who did it.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Those were members of our unit for anti-electronic warfare. In the beginning, it was two soldiers who were tasked with monitoring that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With what equipment?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: The equipment was makeshift. The line was directed from the Zenica post office to one of the offices of the Corps Command, which belonged to the Intelligence Section, and it was -- and the equipment switched on to that particular office allowed to -- allowed the surveillance on the basis of an interphone, and there was a micro-cassette recorder, a micro-tape recorder which was switched on to that appliance. How did we monitor? By directly listening on the conversations, it would be decided whether to go on with the recording during the conversation itself. At any rate, it was all an improvisation. Nothing was automatically done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The microcassettes having been made or having been used in the way you describe, who then reviewed the tape recordings that had been made?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I did it myself mostly, depending on the number of conversations, rather, the frequency of those conversations, but we paid attention to those that had been pointed out to us as more interesting. Then I would listen to them over and over again and make suggestions as to possible further analysis or storage of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you communicate what you heard on the tapes to your senior officers at the time on occasions?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: All conversations of particular interest were interpreted in the original to my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You speak of storage of the recordings. How were they stored?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: As these microcassettes were in very short supply, we decided to record only the most interesting conversations, and the material which I had handed over, that is, when my Commander would ask us to record those conversations, and then I would record that cassette, and you have that cassette now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The cassette of which you speak contained, ultimately, how many different conversations recorded on it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I really cannot give you an accurate number, but there must be about a dozen different conversations involving several persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I lay on the ELMO a document that will become Exhibit 28 -- well, may become Exhibit 2801.3. Further copies will be provided in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what this document is and in whose handwriting it is?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: So this is the jacket of the cassette, and what is written here is the contents or, rather, not the contents, but the sequence of the conversations which were taped on the "A" and the "B" side, with dates, persons engaged in each one of those particular conversations, and it was -- this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The entries on this jacket of the tape, were they made on the dates given or at some date thereafter, and if so, how long after?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: These were after the 25th of February but perhaps a day or two after the 25th of February. It was at that time that I received the order from my Commander to record some conversations which I would think to be of particular interest, and then I decided to do it in this manner. The first conversation which is particularly important was preserved from that period of time; that is, the 23rd or the 24th of January, 1993. Other conversations happened to be on our cassettes at the time. And after I recorded this conversation, I took other conversations also and then copied them over onto this cassette. Naturally, people involved in this, rather, soldiers who did it, they took down the dates, the times, and so on and so forth. What I wrote down was this information that you can find on this cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From what you tell us then, the first conversation of the 24th of January was preserved on a tape until the day, sometime at the end of February, when it was placed as the first recording on the new tape. Can you remember on what sort of tape that 24th of January conversation had been preserved in the meantime or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't remember really, but it must have been a micro-cassette or a cassette of this type, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why was that first conversation of sufficient importance for you to preserve it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: The first conversation shows the intentions of the HVO at the time; that is, who is in command, what are their plans, what they are getting ready to do, who is issuing orders to whom. In view of my job, this conversation was a proper information; that is, it told us what we needed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see, as your evidence explains, that the balance of the tapes start no earlier than the 22nd of February and run on to the 25th. Was that the tapes that you had available, the microtapes that you had available at the time that your superior instructed you to prepare a series of recorded conversations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No. Had we been ordered earlier to keep all that we were recording; we would have tried to find a way to do that. But that order came at a later date, and it was at a later date that he asked us to copy these conversations onto this cassette. This is the way I did it. But at that time we were merely told to store, to keep this conversation because it was of particular significance. Other conversations, I won't say they are of lesser importance or they are unimportant, but they simply happen to be there, so that I recorded a full cassette of this for his needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One last question about that first recording. Was there one particular Commander of yours to whom you reported the existence of this recording?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: The report about the existence of this recording was submitted by me to General Hadzihasanovic, who at that time commanded the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the balance of the conversations recorded, starting on the 22nd of February, give us some examples of the things that you heard on the conversations that justified their being preserved as opposed to discarded in the way that other conversations were discarded. What sort of things justified the keeping of these particular conversations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: If we tried to analyse these conversations, then naturally it would be good to listen to them once again. But these conversations provided us with a lot of information about the situation in the area, the intentions, and among other things we could also see who were the persons directly in command, who were the ones who made decisions, how they organised their system of command and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Even to the extent of picking up by what titles people were referred to?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was curious that about Mr. Blaskic, and I'm referring to that time, at that time he was a Commander, we knew that he was a Colonel, but by the end of these conversations, we could learn that Mr. Kordic also had the rank of a Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having made the tape pursuant to the orders you received, what happened to that tape, in summary? And tell us, please, about any other copies of the tape that were made.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, there were two identical tapes. The jacket of one of them we see here, and another one, identical with this one, I handed over to my Commander, General Hadzihasanovic. What happened to it, I really don't know. But then as I was getting ready to depart for my new post in Vienna, I left a copy of the cassette in the archives to my successor, and I had made that copy at that particular time. And this cassette, the original, if I may call it that, I kept for personal reasons, for reasons of my own, because this is an excellent example both for education and so on. So that at the time when this tape originated, I really could not foresee what would happen to it, but later on I thought it would be good if I kept it as a curio, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this tape that you produced, the tape that is here in the building, the same as the tape provided for the archives and the same as the tape provided to General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first discover that the copy of the tape you had might be of value to this trial?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I discovered it recently. It was in the latter half of November last year when Mr. Mustafa Music came to see me in Vienna. That is, I was about to return and it was a part of my preparations for return, so the activities that we performed in the office in our embassy in Vienna where I worked. During the conversation we had, the question of war crimes came up and documentation about all that and all this, and so we just happened on it by chance. And then I said that -- I say I had just one tape from that period of time, and during our conversation we then thought that this tape might be valuable, because those other copies that I mentioned before were simply missing. And he then asked me to give him that tape, and I gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was it eventually to an investigator called Sue Ellen Taylor and a lawyer called Patrick Lopez-Terres that you identified the tape on the 4th of December, 1999, in Zenica, and that tape you then left with them to bring to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: On that occasion in Zenica, I confirmed that that was indeed the tape which I had handed over. At that time when we talked, they already were in possession of that tape. And as far as I know, they had received it that day or perhaps the day before; that is, that it was officially turned over to them. It wasn't done by me, but I established that that was indeed the tape which I had turned over to my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't imagine there's any issue on the fact that the lawyer and investigator bring the tape properly to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other question before we turn to whether the tape should now be listened to or not at this stage. When did monitoring of the telephone line cease and why?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: We ceased to monitor that particular line, I think, sometime in March. Quite certainly, it was after the talks and conversations, the last ones. I cannot tell you exactly the time, but the reason was quite simple. The communication via that military switchboard became -- was no longer interesting, ceased to be of interest to us, so there was no further reason to monitor the line, so that, quite simply, we gave it up and stopped engaging in that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that stage or at this stage, depending on the nature of the challenge, it may be appropriate to hear the tape or it may be possible to defer listening to the tape until the cross-examination for admissibility reasons is completed. But I can easily see circumstances arising where the issues to be raised might themselves require listening to the tape, but I'm in the Defence hands on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, how much of the tape would you invite us to listen to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you would want, in due course, to hear all of it. There is one conversation which the witness can tell us is really of no value that is very short. The others all turn on matters that are likely to be of value to the Chamber, given the time of the tape-recording and the personalities involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long will it take to play?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The tape takes, I think, about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that we should hear the cross-examination and then decide whether it would be sensible to hear the tape or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Has the tape got an exhibit number, while we're dealing with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The tape's exhibit number is 2801.1. The transcript is 2801.2. Wait there. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Bob Stein. I represent Dario Kordic. If there's any question that I ask you that you don't understand, will you please let me know?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: After 1993, when this tape was made as you described, when did you next listen to the tape, if at all?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to give you a precise answer to that question, but after the tape was made, I listened to that tape immediately after it was made. Later on, I cannot say that it was listened to again, but perhaps several times, yes, but it was no longer of any special importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Those several other times that you may have listened to the tape would have been before 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before 1990 [sic]. So if you're thinking up to the present day, if that's what you mean, I listened to the tape, together with my superior at the time. So when I handed him the tape, we listened to it together. I later on listened to that same tape to ascertain its authenticity, together with Mr. Patrick and Mrs. -- I can't remember her name. I apologise. But anyway, with individuals whom I talked to and to whom I gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to be clear. In 1999 you listened to the tape with your Chief, Mustafa Music; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Then again, did you listen to the entire tape with Mr. Patrick Lopez-Terres and Mrs. Sue Ellen Taylor?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the entire tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At that time or at any other time, did you have a written transcript of the tape?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to the period in which this all started. You actually had a liaison with the PTT company in Zenica, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that liaison was the one who reported that there was something that you might want to hear on one of the phone lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: That conversation came about quite by chance, so it was an individual who did not work directly for us, but when we talked, he happened to offer us the possibility; that is to say, he asked us whether we were interested in anything like that. After that, when I informed my superior, the decision was taken to go ahead with it. So there was no separate information about that line except that it was a military line and that it contained conversations of a military nature, but it was a man who worked at the PTT, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. Perhaps my question wasn't clear. The man who worked at the PTT was liaisoning, that is, co-operating with the 3rd Corps in Zenica relative to interesting conversations. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No. We cannot put it that way, because I do not know what he did at that time and whether he did what you, in fact, stated he was doing. But as I say, we knew each other from before, and he offered us this as a possibility to take up, because while he was working in the post office, he came across this conversation line. Then we put into motion the procedure that I have just explained and decided to go ahead. So he was not an intelligence man for us and didn't do that kind of work alone. So these kinds of activities on his part not did not exist, so I cannot confirm that in the way that you had put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I don't want to quibble with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The Court's attention, if it please the Court, is drawn to the testimony of the witness that was read out earlier in the morning, in which at paragraph 1 he notes: "Part of my duties included liaison with a 3rd Corps in Zenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you one other question parenthetically, and that is: Were you in the public gallery this morning listening to the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And another preliminary question: Do I take of all the conversations that you listened to, you kept only this one tape? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I personally, yes. I kept just that one tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the taping, in this particular situation, started in January of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the first taping occurred on January 24, 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that. Perhaps it started earlier on. I cannot be precise, but the conversation of the 24th of January was saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So you cannot tell us how many conversations before January 24th were discarded?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And can you tell us the exact time of any of these conversations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: If you mean the hours, then I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That is what I mean. Can you tell us, with specificity, the hours of the conversation of the January 24th intercept?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact time, the exact hour, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it between using the index, which I think is to your right on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have -- it might be helpful to have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My understanding is that the Prosecution was going to make extra copies and give it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We only got one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My oversight. I distributed the only ones available without having them adequately copied. If they can be made available to Ms. Verhaag, we'll take it out, and the usher perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You want to cross-examine on it, Mr. Stein. Let it go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. It is on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Between January 24, 1993 and February 22nd, 1993, do I take it you found nothing of interest to record?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I'm sure there were some interesting things, but, unfortunately, nothing was saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And whose decision was it to save or not to save the material coming to you over the phone line?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I could say that I did that. This conversation -- for this conversation, among others, I issued orders that this tape be saved, and the order was principally issued by the Commander. So the other part of the conversation; that is, other conversations which -- just used at the time and not saved for subsequent purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me make sure we understand the process that you were in charge of. There were two other monitors working with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I did not work on it directly, they did. They taped it. They would come -- the end information would come to me; that is to say, the taped conversations. What was urgent we would listen to straightaway. Anything that wasn't vital was not listened to again, but they submitted it in a form of report describing the conversations, the participants in the conversation, and possibly they emphasised whether the conversation would be of interest to us or not. So after that, I would be in a position to either listen to the tape again or not to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right, sir. I think we've gone rather far afield from my question. There were two other individuals also listening to the phone lines besides yourself. True or false?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: At the time, they existed when they were engaged. One man was engaged. It was not able to engage one man to do this job the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In any event, the one man who was listening to the phone call, if he felt it was important, he would record it on a micro-cassette; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the conversations that were considered to be of importance were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
