utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are sorry. This is going much too fast and the quality of the sound is poor indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us simply, at least for this tape, hear the tape. We've got the translation in front of us. Would the interpreters follow with the transcription, and if there are any substantial errors in the transcription, would they point that out at the end of the tape?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is impossible to tell, because if we didn't have the transcript, it could not be interpreted at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's hear at least this version. Let's hear this tape. Could we go on playing it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Let them" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't bother to translate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: From what we could hear, this tape is identical to the transcript that we were given before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, I'm not sure in those circumstances it's going to be a great deal to be gained by going through all these tapes unless there are points which the Prosecution or Defence want us to hear on the tapes, but I'll hear submissions on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm entirely content for the following to happen if this should be acceptable: For the transcript, as is, to be counted as produced; for a couple of supplementary questions to be asked of the witness, in particular whether the names recorded by him on the jacket of the tape are the names that he associated at the time with the people speaking and whether he's able to recognise them; and, thereafter, for the Defence to be provided with a copy of the latest tape so that they can then have the two tapes to compare if they wish to pursue the allegation of corruption between the time of surrender of the tape and today's date; and for the argument then to proceed on the basis of the transcript. But of course, their comparison of the tape won't be able to happen today, but that shouldn't hold up the argument, because the Chamber can work on the basis that there is no corruption revealed by the two tapes, and because it's a Chamber of professional Judges, amended any decision it makes at a later stage if more material comes to hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you sit down, it may be helpful if you just indicated, since you say you've marked them, where the various conversations begin and end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. The second page 1, serial number 908749, is the beginning of what in the witness's statement is referred to as conversation 2 between Kapetanovic and Cosic. Indeed, you can see those names on page 1. That conversation ends on page 2 at line 7, I think. So line 8 can be marked with the number 3, which the witness, in his statement, identifies as a conversation between Grubesic and Blaskic, and that is, again, I think, supported by the content. That conversation ends on page 3, at line 17, I think, and then what follows is conversation number 4, again between Grubesic and Blaskic, and the names can be seen in the transcript itself. That conversation goes over to page 5, at the top, with Blaskic saying, "Good-bye." Then at line 3 is the beginning of conversation number 5, identified as between Blaskic and Kordic, the conversation going on until page 10 at line 15. At line 16, conversation 6, the irrelevant one, as it were, the short one between Ljilja and Boro begins. That conversation ends at the top -- the bottom of page 10 or the top of page 11. So that should be marked as conversation 7 between Grubesic and Blaskic, and that occupies that page. We see at the foot of page 11, "Bye-bye. We'll keep in touch." So the top of page 8 the Chamber could mark 8, the conversation between Blaskic and Kordic. That conversation goes over to page 14, line 9, where you see the beginning of a conversation recorded in the notes of the witness as between Pero and Grubesic. Conversation 9 goes on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not too quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is conversation 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Conversation 9 starts on page 14, line 9, and goes on to page 18, line 25. So that at line 26 or 27, there is the beginning of conversation 10 between Kordic and Blaskic. That conversation goes on to -- and this is the only place where there is some confusion in my mind. I think that conversation goes on probably until the foot of page 18, and is a short conversation, and it may be, and I stress that, it may be that at the very top of page 19 we should write 11, noting that at line 5 there is a change to side B, and observing that in his witness statement, the witness says of conversation 11 that it is continued on side B. I think that that conversation concludes at about line 9, so that from about line 10, but I may be wrong, about line 10 we start off with what is the first of the three conversations listed on side B, therefore, to be marked again with the figure 1. And whether I'm right or wrong about the start point of that conversation, it goes on to page 25, line 13, where there is the beginning -- page 25, line 13, where there's the beginning of the second conversation on side B, said to be between Blaskic and an unidentified person. That conversation goes on to page 31, ending at line 8, and with the third and last conversation starting at line 10, being a conversation between Nakic and Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've not got that last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 31, line 8 is the end of conversation 2, and line 10 the beginning of conversation 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, is there anything you want to ask the witness about these tapes or anything about the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of things, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know if you were following me when I was seeking to identify where the conversation started and finished or not. Were you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I did follow, but in my translation, in my text, the lines are different, the numbers of the lines. But as far as I was able to follow, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second, we've seen your document, which is the cover sheet for the tape itself, which has the names of people said to be speaking in the conversation. We know that the handwriting of that document is yours, but where did you get the names to write down? Was it your own knowledge of the voices, was it a calculation from the contents of the tapes, was it information coming to you from someone else, or how else did you manage to write down these names?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: In most of the cases, the people appearing on the tape and talking say their own names, introduce themselves. So on the basis of previous knowledge, if they give their surname, then we are able to add their names, or vice versa. Another parameter that we used was that we listened to them for some considerable length of time so we could tell by their voices, and we were able to conclude who was doing the speaking. The third way, the third method, was one which I used, that when we listened to the tape repeatedly, we would write down who the participants were, or it would be something that we would decide upon later on when we were not quite sure who it actually was. But after writing down what we considered -- I considered to be valid, we did write this down and it is what was on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The conversation we did hear this afternoon, involving several voices but then principally two voices in conversation, are you able now to recognise those two voices or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Of course, I can. When the real conversation begins, apart from the introduction -- you know, when they just say, "Hello," and so on, I can't tell who they are. But when the conversation begins between the two main speakers, then it's quite obvious who the speakers are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And they were --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: They were Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I don't know if in your version it's got "Voice 6" and "Voice 7." Can you tell us who it was who was speaking of, "Let's burn everything"? Who was that? If you can't remember because you need to listen to it again, you must say so and we'll probably move on. But if you can remember, just tell us who it was.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Voice Number 6 would be Mr. Kordic, and Voice Number 7 would be Mr. Blaskic. But what you have just mentioned, I can't say off the bat. I would have to either read or listen to it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I needn't trouble you with that. One other question that you may be able to help us with, and the Chamber will find this on page 2 at line 29. I'm not sure of the exact reference for this for you on your transcript, but I think it will be on page 2 at line 29 as well. There was a reference by the voice you say was the voice of Kordic to: "... two of our boys killed perfidiously from behind at the checkpoint in Kacuni." Do you now remember any event to which that related; "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: What I can -- I can say "yes," and let me try and explain. Whether I'm right or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What is it you can remember, then, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I remember that on many occasions there were problems with those checkpoints, but I know that at that time there were talks concerning these checkpoints and demands were made that they be dismantled, and the European Monitors were also included in these events. Now, as far as this particular incident is concerned, I cannot say whether it was on that date or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident like this having happened?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I remember this particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honour, I think there may be other evidence of that already before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other passage I would like you to have a look at on your document is at page 4, and it's line 17, I think. In the English version, it's at page 4, line 25. You may not have listened to this particular tape or part of the tape for some time, but you spoke this morning of Kordic being addressed and/or referred to as "Colonel." Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that one individual speaks about that, that Mr. Kordic has the rank of Colonel. I don't know which of the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at your page 4, line 17, I'm only asking if this is the place you have in mind? It's our English page 4, line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The numbers have been cut off our pages. You are, I assume, referring to ten lines up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness, do you have page -- there are two pages 4, so give me the copy and I'll hand you mine, actually, and I'll mark it. Look at this marked version, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC
utterances.text: As far as this is concerned, I couldn't say whether that is that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. There may be another reference, and we'll find that later. That's all I need to ask the witness in relation to the tapes at this stage on the issue of admissibility, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What else do you want to ask him generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably nothing actually generally, either. If we're dealing with an admissibility topic, nothing else, and the tapes really speak for themselves because he's identified the witnesses, he's told us the generality of what the tapes reveal, and it will be possible for the Chamber to read the transcripts to themselves in due course or tell us to have them read out in full so that there's a public hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll deal with the admissibility point now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, just to clarify, I think you'll find, with regard to the last point made by Mr. Nice and the witness, the reference on page 4 of the English, line 25, to the word "Colonel" does not appear in the Croatian version which accompanied this translation to us. With regard to admissibility and with regard to the manner in which you can compare the tape which the witness has brought with him today, let me suggest the following: If that tape is, having now been given to the Court, copied to us, we could take on the task which we proposed to do at lunch, but there was not enough time, to compare that which is before us now, the fourth version of the tape, to the third version of the tape, and we'll see whether issues are resolved or made more difficult. I think they'll be made more difficult, and the proof of that is if you look at the index, 2801.3, the index has "Side A" and "Side B." The "A" side, the first entry is the January 24, '93, Kordic/Blaskic conversation. That's the first thing on this tape, and it's on side A and it's clear. Yet the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Stein. One minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, this isn't a very satisfactory position in which we find ourselves. There are now two versions of the tape, one of which we have with a transcript; the other one, we don't. Now, we need to know what the difference between the two is, if any, and we have in mind inviting our translators to look at this as promptly as possible to resolve, if there are any differences. And once we've done that, we will rule upon the subject. I am going to ask the Legal Officer something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's not satisfactory, as I've said. In fact, it's highly unsatisfactory. But what we're going to have to do is to order that this second tape be transcribed and any differences between this and the original be noted, in whichever way seems appropriate, and any differences between the transcript and the new tape be noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in Your Honour's hands. This all arose because of the nature of the allegation made. I know that this exercise is likely to take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long did it take to get a translation last time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it was over Christmas, but it took over a month altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be dealt with as a priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we shall order that that be done. Now, we cannot keep the witness here or ask him to come back, so any examination which anybody has on any aspect of the tape that they would want to ask, outside the admissibility question, covering any aspect, had better be done now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness. I do, at some stage, have a few arguments on the question of admissibility, but maybe I can defer those, indeed, until after the witness has withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, or until after we know what the answer to the tape is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My position is the same. I have no further questions of the witness. Should we not prevail on the admissibility issue, then I would ask that the cross-examination be incorporated by reference on issues of weight as opposed to admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean we don't have to have a distinct phase here between the arguments as to admissibility and the substantive trial. It's all part of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And I do have a few comments as well relative to admissibility, if Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you've got no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, that concludes your evidence. There are no further questions. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres will withdraw with the witness. And, of course, the witness has surrendered what is his only remaining copy of the tape, so we will arrange, by one means or another, that he has a copy to take with him, because he has an interest in retaining it. The next witness is in the building and is ready to give evidence, but we weren't sure how long was going to be taken. It may take just a couple of minutes to find him, and indeed Ms. Somers, who's going to take him. While that's happening, the position about the map is probably worth ventilating. The Chamber will recall requiring the front-line maps. They were provided fairly swiftly. The person who provided those maps has done a great deal of further work to both check his original works, to correct it, and to provide more detail. The amended maps have now been served, I think today. The amendments are, I think, comparatively modest, but supporting material is considerable in quantity. I've had two approaches today, one from Mr. Kovacic, with the helpful suggestion that it might be possible to negotiate between the parties to see where the common ground is and to see what, if anything, remains outstanding for dispute. I hope I correctly summarised his position, although he was going to talk to Mr. Lopez-Terres about it in more detail. On the other hand, I understand there may be a more root and branch problem raised by those representing Mr. Kordic. They're concerned, indeed, about the expertise of the witness, and also concerned about the reliance he has placed on answers that Blaskic gave in his trial. It seems to me that on this particular topic, without prejudice to any other arguments about Blaskic testimony, the witness has simply done the best he can on the available information to try and draw front-line maps identifying where he has got his information from, information that is necessarily hearsay if he wasn't there in the field himself. So that to draw material from Blaskic's evidence in trial is hardly inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this arises out of a request that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was a matter which was of interest to me, and I thought might be useful for the trial and would assist me in understanding the trial, and to take narrow points on admissibility doesn't seem, to me, to be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any case, I do accept that the Defence have been provided with a great deal of material only today to consider, but the material is simply the supporting material. They must know from their own instructions, in relation to the vast majority of the points that are on the maps and in indeed in the accompanying report, they must know whether it's accurate or inaccurate, and it should be possible for them to focus the points of dispute pretty narrowly. Now, we've got a witness today, and I know we've got another witness for tomorrow, but I would ask that Mr. Elford, at the very least, be accommodated for the purposes of giving the evidence in chief this week, assuming we have time for him, and he can present his maps, for which we have a board in court, and explain his findings. And I'm sure the Defence will have had an opportunity by then to consider the supporting material and to cross-examine him as far as that may be necessary. I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. May it please the Court. I do want to address the Court at some time about the admissibility of the tape, and I have a few points to make but I won't do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it maybe more convenient, unless there's some particular point you want us to deal with now, to deal with all the arguments when we know what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fine. Not a problem. Relative to Mr. Elford and the maps, we, yesterday, were given his report. A brief read clearly shows that he's talking about troop strength, troop movements, front lines, perfectly relevant things, but he's doing it from the perspective of an expert or someone who has compiled expert evidence, and it has not been given to us in adequate time to prepare, nor are we given the requisite number of days under the Rule. Moreover, it's not been given to us in a language the accused can understand. But beyond that, we have been given today the backup material for this report, and it includes -- it includes -- the backup material for these maps includes statements of General Blaskic, to be sure an interesting issue, but a lot of milinfosums. We've tried to figure out the ones we've never seen before quickly last night. There seemed to be at least a dozen, if not more. So the report and the map together are based on brand new information for us, indeed information we've been looking for for some time. It may be that when all is said and done, and these ultimately may be exactly consistent with our theory, or at least close enough, we can negotiate. But we're not at that point, having been given volumes of material yesterday and today as to the Blaskic issue, because this is going to come up again and again. It is our considered judgement that unless or until we have all of Colonel Blaskic's testimony, including that which was given in closed session, and all of the exhibits, we can't pick part of his testimony and just choose part. If the Prosecution wants to call Colonel Blaskic, they may do so, as apparently is our right. But to take his evidence in the parts they like and use it in support here and in other situations, it's in the binders, it's in some other international armed conflict issues, it's coming more and more, is unfair to us because with a unitary Prosecutor they know it all. They know everything that he said during the course of his trial. We may agree or disagree with some or part, but we're not in a position to know. If we had it all, then we might say, "We'll stipulate to all of it or part of it." But to use his --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Stein slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: -- his testimony in support of this witness's maps and conclusion, in our view, would be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, what have you got from the transcript of Blaskic? What have you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. We have his open session testimony. Anything that's made public we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't have closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Correct. And he testified for 30 days, as you recall. I'm not sure how many days were in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How much of it have you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: How much of the 30 days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I don't know off the top of my head, sir. I just don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want the closed session testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have to remind me. Have you asked for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I know we asked for the closed session testimony of one if not both of the court witnesses that were called, in a prior application. I don't believe we've specifically asked, although I could stand to be corrected, about General Blaskic's testimony. The issue of his being used by the Prosecution is a relatively new one. As I'm standing here I'm trying to think back, and I have a vague memory of this coming up, but I'm sorry, sir, it's just not leaping to the front of my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree with the thoughts conveyed by my learned friend Mr. Stein regarding the totality of Blaskic's testimony. That should be provided to us as one of the sources on the basis of which an expert person can reconstruct the positions of the conflicting parties. That is only one source. And of course, the totality of that testimony would be desirable, rather than having only parts of it. However, it is my opinion that we need to think about something else. Today, again, we are confronting a highly peculiar situation. I consider it to be specific as compared to customary procedure, even in this Court. The value of evidence, the parties, the provenance of evidence and so on, but I won't theoretise. I would rather say the following: As far as I have been able to understand my colleagues, this material, this evidence, the maps and the supporting material on which the maps were drafted, were compiled by a professional person -- I don't know exactly what qualifications he has -- but is formally a member of the Prosecution team in this case, which means that a party has prepared a piece of evidence and produced it in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What can the objection be to this? I find these whole proceedings confrontational. Now, this should be a straightforward matter to agree a map or not agree it. I find it hard to believe that there cannot be agreement about something as straightforward as that. If it said the lines vary, let us find out how it is that the lines vary, but points are taken the whole time in the most confrontational way. The fact that the witness comes from the investigators doesn't matter. It's the weight of the evidence. Now, we've got a witness outside. I suggest that what we do is get on with him rather than waste further time about these maps. I shall instruct counsel to discuss the matter over the adjournment and find how best to deal with a matter which I raised, because it would be of assistance to the court, and I would be grateful if we could have that assistance put before us in the most straightforward way, rather than constant arguments about admissibility. Mr. Kovacic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but it's time that we moved on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may, that was the direction in which I was heading, because the situation is specific. I am not quite sure that we understand who is who and what the value of things are, because I think, going on the basis of what you have said, if the Prosecutor is preparing evidence, it would be the same as if I were to testify. I was going to ask you if I could give certain instructions as to whether that presentation is considered to be evidence in the classical formal sense, or is it merely a means to portray things? If it is the latter, and it seems to me to be somewhere in between, in our view, it would be more practical, more sensible, and more economical in time if we could discuss with the Prosecutor, in a constructive fashion, which other sources need to be taken into consideration for the maps to be drafted correctly. I personally think, on the basis of what I have looked through, that 80 percent at least of the material is more or less unchallenged. I think a small additional effort would be needed, and the willingness of the Prosecutor to accept some other sources, our own and from the Blaskic case, then we would have a far greater degree of certainty. Otherwise, we will be wasting time on the cross-examination, and we will have to produce the same evidence in our own defence case, bring experts, draw from the Blaskic evidence, and so on. Some of these things may be important, others not, but clearly this does not provide a complete picture. I think the proposal is a constructive one. Could you give us certain limits? Is this classical evidence or is it simply a presentation? If it is a presentation, as a summary of the evidence at the disposal of the Prosecution, taken from other cases, then perhaps we could make our contribution to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have in mind an agreed document that is put before the Court. If, as appear possible, it is not going to be practicable to agree anything in this case, then we'll have to find some other way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, and I join my colleague Judge May, that it is necessary for you, amongst yourselves, outside the courtroom, that is, between the Defence and the Prosecution, as you have proposed anyway and as Mr. Nice has mentioned, to find a maximum number of points of agreement. On the points that you are not in agreement, you can mention them, if you insist, saying, "Here are the points on which we agree, here is the point of the Defence, on such and such a point, whereas the Prosecution is of such and such an opinion." But we need to know what are the points of agreement, mentioning at the same time points of disagreement, and in that way we will not use too much time. Try and find a common denominator. Then regarding the elements of disagreement, mention them. Tell us about them. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. But, Your Honour, please. We have to be practical. I'm sorry to be wasting -- taking up your time. We got the maps a month ago. We couldn't engage in a serious analysis of those maps until we received the author's material, supporting material. We got it yesterday. It is excellently well written, logically, and fine in every respect, but in the footnotes, the sources are indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you need for all this? Tell the Court. Tell us, how much time do you need to examine all these papers? We're not pressuring anyone here, including you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we got this today. I don't even know how much of it I have to study. I cannot, in all sincerity, tell you 20 days or 100 days. Give me at least 24 hours to look through this pile to be able then to tell you whether we need 10 days, 15 days, a reasonable amount of time. Of course, you are aware also of the amounts of material we have received in the last month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I think I agree with you. Will you -- both of us -- both Mr. Stein and yourself, tell us tomorrow how much time -- in the course of the day -- tell us in the course of the day how much time you will need, because, in the meantime, you will at least have an opportunity to look through the documents and be able to tell us. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I am ready to give you an estimate tomorrow. If I can have up to Friday, that would be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Friday. Yes. Now, we're going to hear a witness, but before we do, Mr. Stein, you could help with something else. I have in mind the matter we were dealing with, the new tape, and your suggestion that you might listen to it or those instructing you. What I'm concerned about is the fact that it took a month to get the last translation, and it could well be a long time before we get a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, if it was possible for you to listen to it and give us at least a preliminary view on it. If you accept it, for instance, you could say so, or if there are substantial areas of disagreement, you could point them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it may be, with the Prosecution, between you you could come up with a quicker answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I suggested that. Over lunch we were doing a lot of things. I would be delighted to do that, take that burden on and then we could report whether there are disparities or not, and what they are, show them to the Prosecution. They can do a double-check and present it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be a more practical way of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I would be glad to take -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Meanwhile, we will ask the translators how long they would need to do this, if, as we suggest, they do it as a matter of priority, and then you perhaps can tell us in the next day or two what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll be glad to. And we'll also tell you our position on the readiness for the maps, although, I would probably -- I'll be specific tomorrow, but we'll probably need the break period to finally resolve that. The reason is, and you should know this, we now have the Prosecution seeking to admit the testimony of 41 witnesses from other cases. The span of testimony is about 12.700 pages. So you can see we are very busy. Not that I mind being busy, but I wasn't hyperbolising when we talked about two metres of paper. So we are ploughing through it. That's all I have to say now. I'll save it for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear about the maps on Friday. And if you, at some stage, need a reading day, I'm not encouraging you, but if you do, will you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We're looking forward to next week and a change in my glasses thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's begin the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you state your complete name.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Mirsad Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: The 12th of September, 1968.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: An electronics technician for telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Though you were born in Zenica, where did your family live in Central Bosnia up until 1993? What was the principal city of residence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: We lived in Vitez, in the town of Vitez, and I was born in Zenica, merely because the maternity ward was in Zenica at the time, the maternity hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court about your military experience?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: You mean before 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. Your complete military experience from the 1980s onward.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I did my regular military service in the Yugoslav People's Army in September 1987 until September 1988. After that, in 1992, sometime in June, I was mobilised to the Territorial Defence, and I was there, which later became the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, until roughly the 30th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were with the Territorial Defence on approximately 20th of October, 1992, when it had to abandon its headquarters in the high school in Vitez and relocate to Stari Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you very briefly state why the headquarters changed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I think the main reason was that that was the only place in town. For the HVO to have full control of the town, we had to leave it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there any attacks to speak of by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a rather strong attack. Actually, it was a rocket fired from a rocket launcher. It wasn't a real attack. Also, there was some shooting at the school from automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your residence is in Vitez. Can you describe where you and your family lived?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Our house was in the centre of town, one could say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it a house or an apartment in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: It was an apartment building in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have a house anywhere in the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had a house, a family home, newly built.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: It's called Zume or Ahmici. It depends. Some people call it one, some the other. These are close by.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever occupy that house?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was anyone occupying that house in Ahmici on 16 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a family there from Karaule, I think their surname was Memeledzija, as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were they occupying the house with the consent of your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What happened to that family on April 16th, 1993, specifically in the course of the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we saw them later on. The women were immediately taken to a camp at the railway station, and the men hid, because close to the house was a kind of auxiliary building with a cellar, and they hid there, covered themselves with a kind of cover. And as my mother kept some food there, they were able to feed themselves there for a couple of days in this cellar, which was about one and a half by one and a half metres in size.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What happened to that house, to your house in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: The house was set alight that very same morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not the Memeledzija family was in the house at the time it was set alight?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: No one was in the house. The main members of the family were in this outhouse , in a kind of cellar that we had where we kept some foodstuffs. So no one was in the house itself. The women were taken to a camp, and the men were in this outhouse in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: One last question about this house. Do you have any idea as to who may have set the house ablaze?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, how is the witness going to know this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It will come across as not being direct; it will be what is referred to as hearsay, if the Court is willing to accept the witness's rendition in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you can lay the foundations for it, please, Ms. Somers, first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you personally hear any comment about who may have set the house ablaze?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Something that could serve as an indication was a conversation that my father had with Mr. Memeledzija, when the latter said that he heard, as the house was set ablaze, that there were two men -- of course, he couldn't see them -- and their conversation was roughly as follows: "Set the house alight." And he said, "No, you do it. You were his friend."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Discussing your own situation on 16 April 1993, what happened in Vitez, where you were?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, we were woken up by the explosions about 5.30 in the morning. Of course, we had no knowledge as to what might happen. For security reasons, we hid in the basement of the building, which had previously been prepared for that purpose, ever since the bombing from the air.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to say from which direction the shelling was coming? Is there any way you could have detected that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: You see, the explosions could be heard. They were close by. That was clear. So it could roughly come from the region of Stari Vitez, because our building is about 150 to 200 metres away from it as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was it Stari Vitez which was being shelled, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I think it was, among other places. Explosions could be heard from other parts of the town as well, but as this was very close, these were the ones we heard best.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: While you were in the basement of your apartment building, were you approached by any persons or were you able to remain there undisturbed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: No. Two or three hours later, soldiers appeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What kind of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms, with black masks over their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From which Army?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: They were Vitezovi, HVO Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how were you able to identify that they were Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: On their sleeves they had the patches of Vitezovi, and we were all familiar with those patches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did they also bear HVO patches?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They always had both patches, the HVO and the Vitezovi. I think one was on one shoulder and the other on the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you in any way able to determine the identity of any of these masked HVO Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I identified one of them by his voice. We knew each other well, so I had no difficulty in recognising his voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: His name was Robert Safradin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Safradin and the others ask of you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: They asked for weapons, and they threatened should they find anything in anybody's apartment, that they would be killed. And he said that only the Turks should watch out, not the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there others in the basement with you or were there only members of the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: No, all the tenants of that building were there or, rather, of that entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does that mean that there were Serbs and Croats as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did Safradin make any comments to you about what territory the HVO may have had or was interested in?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: After that incursion of theirs into the basement, if I can call it that, we went outside. I asked when would all this stop, because we had no idea that anything like this could happen. We had had two clashes before, and we thought that this was like one of those. And he said, roughly, "Today we're clearing out Stari Vitez, and then only Grbavica will be left."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know who Safradin's superiors were?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: By chance, as he was a member of the Vitezovi, I know that there was Darko Kraljevic, Niko and Jakov Krizanac, and some others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry, what was the last name of Niko?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Krizanac, and Jakov Krizanac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you yourself know Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you remain in the basement or did you go elsewhere with Safradin and his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I called them in, mainly in the interests of my own family, and for things to calm down I invited them to go to my apartment, to have a drink together for them, to rest for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did they keep their masks on?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: When we started climbing the steps and when we reached the apartment, all three of them took off their masks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you confirm it was, in fact, Safradin?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The morning of April 19th or thereabouts, were you taken from your apartment building, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. A group of members of the Military Police, I think they were, came with a van.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Whose Military Police, which Army?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: HVO, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: And they told us roughly this: that in the interests of our own personal security, it would be better for us to go with them because some soldiers coming from the front line might be irritated and that something could happen to us. So the reason -- explanation given to us was that it was in the interests of our personal security.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And which group of persons were they addressing? Were they all women, children; can you be specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe I said I can't remember exactly whether those from 17 to 65 or from 18 to 60. I don't know exactly. But there was an age limit to it, because I know that a neighbour was left behind simply because he was beyond that age limit. But whether it was 17 to 60 or what was it, I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And were they only men in this age group or were they also women?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, only men, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you go to the SDK building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's where they took us straight by a van.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Once you got to SDK, were you free to leave or were you detained?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: We were imprisoned there, and when we arrived that area was already half full, I mean in the SDK, and we were kept there. We were detained and could not leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You say "half full." Half full of what type of person? Who was being kept there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, I should say that they were all, I mean, Bosniaks, Muslims, within that age range somewhere between 18 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Also only men?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know the name "Zabac"?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Zabac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: He's a bloke from Vitez. His nickname was Zabac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was his real name?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know his real first name, but his surname was Kovac. I really don't know. I can't remember. But he was -- he was a well-known person in Vitez, because he used to play football and he played for the local club, and everybody knew him, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have any observation about Zabac's role in the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: My impression is that he was one of the people who commanded, one of the Commanders, because he would come from time to time in an HVO Military Police vehicle, and the guards who were there for us would ask him various questions such as when would another shift come and things like that. So that is where I gained the impression that he was one of the Commanding Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it your observation that he was in the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the Military Police, because -- and in any event, he had the insignia, he had a white belt. And that vehicle -- I also knew that vehicle, and I knew that it was a vehicle that was used by the guys from the HVO Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you personally know Mario Cerkez? If not, how did you come to know about him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I did not know him personally, but it was owing to the local television. I think it was the -- I think that was the first time that he appeared there as an HVO Officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you able to identify what his role was in the HVO, of what, if anything, he commanded, or what he commanded?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I think that afterwards -- that is, when I saw him first, I simply did not pay any attention to what his role might be or his function, but subsequently I think he figured as a Brigade Commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know his relationship to Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't really know what the relationship was. That is, I do not have any definite pros or cons in one or the other direction. But on the basis of what I knew and what I know now about the HVO structure and the organisation of Herceg-Bosna as a whole, I believe that the relationship was very close and that there was kind of a subordination relationship between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was subordinate to whom, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I think that Cerkez was a superior. I believe that Kraljevic -- well, at least I knew him personally, and I do not think he really would have been able to do certain things by himself, for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For how long were you detained in the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: I think it must have been some 15 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And during those 15 days, were you taken to do any forced labour?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was that labour?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, we were mostly taken to dig trenches and arrange these military facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: During that particular period, where were the trenches located?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, what I know is where I was. The first time, it was a group of about five or six of us, and we were taken to an area below the village of Vranjska. Its name should be Rijeka, and we were there awhile and then we were taken to the area of Kratine, which is below Kuber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: These locations are both in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Discussing Kratine, was the situation involving an active or not a terribly active front line?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: The fire hardly ever stopped from both sides. There was shelling from time to time. But fighting, that is, attacks on one side on the other, no, as far as I know, there were none at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Perhaps I was less than clear. Was your trench-digging at Kratine on an active, dangerous front line?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. That, yes, because bullets were whistling by around us. Fortunately, nobody was hit, and even those shells were falling not too far from us, and fire was a common phenomenon during those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is Kratine anywhere near Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. You go to Kratine from Nadioci. How far that is, I wouldn't know, but perhaps a kilometre or two, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you were taken to Kratine, who was the HVO person in charge of Kratine?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Our first encounter, the person we met first was somebody who was called Cicko. I believe his last name was Bralo, but I know we all called him Cicko. He was the first man to see us up there, and he appeared to be some kind of a Commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what particular aspect of your existence at Kratine did he control?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: By and large, the part which had to do with our accommodation, or perhaps food, and various types of ill treatment, if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is Ivica Vujica?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Ivica Vujica at that time, that is, precisely at that time, they called him the Front Line Commander or the Front Commander, so that should mean the Commander of that Sector. I don't know. I don't know how long that particular front line segment was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was he also at Kratine?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry, what was your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, when you get to a convenient moment. It's after 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any special units that Ivica Vujica was a member of?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD AHMIC
utterances.text: He had a flash -- a patch of Jokers on his sleeve, so that there was no dilemma as to what unit he belonged. After all, nobody tried to conceal the fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is a convenient moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just let me deal with two matters. Tomorrow there will be an extended luncheon adjournment from half past 1.00 [sic] to half past 2.00. The other matter is more long-term, and that is about the dates. I mention it now. We have in mind at the moment beginning the Defence on the 10th of April. That will mean that there will be a month between Prosecution and Defence. However, the Defence will thereafter have two weeks, beginning the 17th of April and the 24th of April, additional which the Court will not be sitting. We shall resume on the 2nd of May. Those dates may be subject to change, but at the moment everyone should work on that basis. Did I say "half past 1"? Half past 12 to half past 2 tomorrow. Mr. Ahmic, could you be back, please, tomorrow at half past 9. Could you remember this in the adjournment and any others there may be: Don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and don't let anybody speak to you about it, and that does include the members of the Prosecution. So would you be back, please, at half past 9 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
